introduction: The inner life has consequences. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes thoughts that become realities from idle fancies; calls a good intention a lighted candle and the root of the tree of deeds; says that thoughts pass from mind to mind; and gives a test for telling inspiration from imagination, which is agreement with the revealed texts. He quotes the tradition that a person’s intention is better than his act. Proverbs, the Dhammapada and the Gospels teach that a person is what he thinks in his heart; the saying of Muḥammad on intentions is given, with David’s unbuilt temple, Paul’s “willing mind,” and Kant’s good will that shines like a jewel. Shakespeare supplies two lines on what imagination can do to a mind. The cautions come from the parable of the two sons and from James, for whom intention without the deed is dead, and from Emerson, who trusted the inner gleam above every text.
questions: “Sound and true conceptions … when combined with resolution, become outwardly realized.” Recall an idea of yours that became real and one that did not. What made the difference?
“A man’s intention is better than his act.” In what sense? Put the two sons of Jesus’ parable beside the tradition.

How is inspiration to be told from imagination? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá gives the test of the texts; Emerson says to watch the gleam within. What would you do with a strong inner conviction that had no support in scripture?
Evil thoughts “come from other minds; they are reflected,” and good ones spread “like doves of peace.” If thoughts travel, what responsibility does a person have for what he dwells on?
Imagination can overpower even a scientific mind. Where is imagination a danger in religious life, and where is it needed?

outside.why: Contemplation yields “two kinds of conceptions”: sound ones that are realized, and “vain thoughts and useless ideas.” Theseus in A Midsummer Night’s Dream on the faculty that does both: the lunatic, the lover and the poet are of imagination all compact; it gives to airy nothing a local habitation and a name.
Thought is treated as the measure of the person in the oldest wisdom books. Proverbs: as he thinketh in his heart, so is he.
“A good intention is like a lighted candle - its rays spread in all directions.” Jesus: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
“The more thought expands, the greater becomes one’s inclination toward” higher things. The Dhammapada: all that we are is the result of what we have thought.
Their bodies linger on earth “but their spirits travel in the immensity of space.” Paul: our conversation is in heaven.
“To be without insight is verily a great defect.” Jesus: if ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.
“Inspiration is in conformity with the Divine Texts, but imaginations do not conform therewith.” The First Letter of John: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.
Jeremiah on those who took the one for the other: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the Lord.

The test of an inner prompting is the revealed text. Emerson wanted no outside test: a man should learn to detect and watch that gleam of light which flashes across his mind from within, more than the lustre of the firmament of bards and sages. What has each of them seen go wrong?

“Unless there is good intention … the tree of deeds will not yield fruits.” Kant on what gives an act its worth: a good will, even if it should achieve nothing, would, like a jewel, still shine by its own light.
Jesus on where deeds begin: out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites a tradition that “a man’s intention … is better than his act.” The best-known saying of Muḥammad on the subject: the reward of deeds depends upon the intentions.
A good intention is credited even when the act is impossible. David wished to build the temple and was not allowed: thou didst well that it was in thine heart.

Intention is better than act. Jesus told of two sons, one who said “I go, sir” and went not, and one who refused and afterward went, and asked: whether of them twain did the will of his father? When does a good intention count, and when is it the first son’s answer?

James would add a caution: as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that a true intention cannot fail to seek its act. How do you tell an intention from a wish?
“The day of goodly words, goodly deeds, and good thoughts.” Paul: whatsoever things are true, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report, think on these things.
“Good intentions and sound thoughts attract confirmations.” Paul: if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.

“Pure intention and righteous deeds influence stones and rocks.” A psalm asks that the inward part be right first: let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight.
Unwanted evil thoughts “come from other minds”; one should not become a mirror for them. Paul: bringing into captivity every thought.
And what steadies a mind against them. Isaiah: thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee.

“No matter how scientific a man may be, yet at times ‘imagination’ gains a power over his mind,” as when he fears to sleep beside a corpse. Hamlet: there is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.

kings-thou-didst-well-that-it-was-in-thi.text: And it was in the heart of David my father to build an house for the name of the Lord God of Israel. And the Lord said unto David my father, Whereas it was in thine heart to build an house unto my name

proverbs-as-he-thinketh-in-his-heart.text: For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he

corinthians-every-thought-into-captivity.text: Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ

jeremiah-vision-of-their-own-heart.text: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the Lord
